B01.name: STATIC T-B01 black-retired-teacher
B01.headline: Retired teachers: finally play piano songs you love
B01.message:
You spent your whole career helping other people learn. This time, it's your turn.

Thirty-odd years of lesson plans, marking and parents' evenings. You know better than anyone that a bright student can still give up if they're taught in the wrong order. Start with the dull part, promise the good part "later", and you lose them.

That's exactly what happened to most adults and the piano. Including, maybe, you.

Stephen Ridley plays street pianos and packed concert halls around the world. He'll tell you it was never about talent. Everything he does at a piano comes down to one thing: understanding how songs are actually built.

This might annoy a few people who taught music the traditional way. But any good teacher will recognise it: the method matters more than the student. Begin with the songs people love and they keep coming back. Begin with drills and they drift away.

This is for you if you taught for a living and the time is finally yours. If there's a piano you always meant to get to, and a song you always meant to play on it, once the marking was done. The marking is done.

Most piano courses for adults are built like a textbook nobody would choose to read. Chapter one, exercises. Chapter five, maybe a tune. As a teacher, you'd never design a lesson that way. You'd start with what the learner cares about.

Worried it's too late? Cyd, a retired college teacher, started at 70 and calls the method "first rate". Marie started at 62 and calls learning "a joy".

It's called the Ridley Method, and Stephen is teaching it himself, live, for ninety minutes.

In the class you'll see:

• Why the order you learn in matters more than talent
• The simple idea hiding inside the songs you already love
• What your left hand is actually for (nobody explains this)
• How to play by feel, without decoding a page
• A ten-minutes-a-day habit that fits a retired week

It's free and it's live. You don't need a piano to join. Bring a pen, some paper and the one song you've always wanted to play.

B02.name: STATIC T-B02 black-retired-nurse
B02.headline: Retired nurses: the piano songs you love, finally
B02.message:
Nurses spend a whole career looking after everyone else. Then one day, the shifts stop.

Night shifts. Double shifts. Christmases on the ward and birthdays you missed. For years there was no room for anything that was just for you, and you got used to that.

Now there's room. And a lot of retired nurses find that the thing they quietly want to fill it with is music. Sitting at a piano, playing a song they love, for nobody but themselves.

Stephen Ridley plays street pianos and packed concert halls around the world. He'll tell you it was never about talent. Everything he does at a piano comes down to one thing: understanding how songs are actually built.

Here's something nurses already know from the job. You didn't learn it all from a textbook. You learned by doing, with someone showing you how it really works on the ward. Piano is the same. You learn by playing songs, not by memorising pages first.

This is for you if you nursed for years and now have time back. If you've always loved music but never had the hours, and somewhere along the way you decided it was too late. It isn't.

Most piano courses expect you to sit through months of exercises before you play anything you'd want to hear. After a career of hard work, you don't need more homework. You need something that feels good from the first week.

Worried about your age? Marie started at 62 and calls learning "a joy". Cyd started at 70 and calls the method "first rate".

It's called the Ridley Method, and Stephen is teaching it himself, live, for ninety minutes.

In the class you'll see:

• How to start on a song you love, not a page of exercises
• The simple pattern hiding inside most of the music you know
• What your left hand is actually for
• How to play by feel, the way you learned on the job
• How ten minutes a day is enough, even on tired days

It's free and it's live. You don't need a piano to join. Bring a pen, some paper and the one song you've always wanted to play.

B03.name: STATIC T-B03 black-grandparent
B03.headline: Play the piano for your grandkids, not just for you
B03.message:
"Can you play something?" Most grandparents have to say no. Imagine being the one who says yes.

Picture the grandkids squeezed next to you on the piano bench. You play a song they know. They sing along, a bit too loud. Then they ask for it again. And again.

That's the kind of memory a child keeps for the rest of their life. Long after the toys are gone, they'll remember the grandparent who played the piano.

Stephen Ridley plays street pianos and packed concert halls around the world, and the people who stop to listen are often grandparents with little ones on their shoulders. He'll tell you it was never about talent. It comes down to one thing: understanding how songs are actually built.

This might surprise you. Your grandkids don't care if you can read music. They don't care about grades or exams. They care that you can sit down and play the song they love. That's a much shorter road than anyone told you.

This is for you if there are grandchildren in your life, or soon will be, and you'd love to be the one at the piano when the family comes round. The birthday song. The Christmas songs. The tune from their favourite film.

Most piano courses start you with exercises no child has ever asked to hear. By the time you get to the songs, the grandkids have grown up. You don't have years to wait, and you don't need them.

Never played at all? Neither had John. "I never played piano before in my life," John wrote. Now John plays a Roland keyboard and calls it "a blast".

It's called the Ridley Method, and Stephen is teaching it himself, live, for ninety minutes.

In the class you'll see:

• How to start a song your grandkids will sing along to
• The simple idea underneath the songs every family knows
• What your left hand is for, so it sounds full, not thin
• Why you don't need to read music to play for them
• How ten minutes a day gets you there faster than you think

It's free and it's live. You don't need a piano to join. Bring a pen, some paper and the one song you've always wanted to play.

B04.name: STATIC T-B04 black-piano-nobody-plays
B04.headline: That piano nobody plays? Here's how to finally use it
B04.message:
There's a piano in your house. The lid has been closed for years.

Maybe it was your mother's. Maybe you bought it the year you were finally going to learn. It's still there in the corner, photos on top, gently going out of tune. Guests sometimes ask, "Do you play?" and you laugh and say, "Not really."

Every time you walk past it, there's a little voice: one day.

Stephen Ridley plays all sorts of pianos, from battered street uprights to grand pianos in packed concert halls. He'll tell you the instrument was never the problem. Everything comes down to one thing: understanding how songs are actually built.

Here's what nobody tells people with a silent piano at home. The piano isn't waiting for you to get better at reading music. It's waiting for you to play one song you love on it. That's a much smaller step than it looks from across the room.

This is for you if there's a piano in your home that nobody plays. If it was meant to be filled with music and somehow never was. And if there's one song you've always wanted to hear coming from it.

Most people with a quiet piano tried once. A teacher, a book, an app. It started with exercises, it felt like homework, and the lid went down again. That wasn't you failing. That was the wrong way in.

Never played a note? Neither had John. "I never played piano before in my life," John wrote. Now John plays and calls it "a blast".

It's called the Ridley Method, and Stephen is teaching it himself, live, for ninety minutes.

In the class you'll see:

• How to start the song you've always wanted to hear on that piano
• The simple idea hiding inside most of the music you love
• What your left hand is actually for
• How to play by feel, without a book open on the stand
• Why ten minutes a day is enough to open that lid for good

It's free and it's live. You don't need a piano to join. Bring a pen, some paper and the one song you've always wanted to play.

B05.name: STATIC T-B05 black-quit-as-a-kid
B05.headline: Quit piano as a kid? Why that wasn't your fault
B05.message:
You didn't quit piano as a kid because you weren't musical. Here's what really happened.

The exercise books. The drills. The practice chart on the fridge. The teacher who sighed when you got it wrong. And the music you actually loved, the songs on the radio, was always for "later".

So you stopped. And you decided you "just weren't musical". You've carried that around ever since.

Stephen Ridley plays street pianos and packed concert halls around the world. He'll tell you it was never about talent. Everything he does at a piano comes down to one thing: understanding how songs are actually built.

This might annoy anyone who still believes in the old way. But the kids who quit piano weren't the unmusical ones. Most of them were the ones who wanted to play real music and were handed drills instead. Wanting the songs was never a weakness.

This is for you if you had lessons as a kid and quit. If you still remember a few bars of something. If part of you has wished, every time you hear someone play, that you'd kept going.

You were taught in the wrong order. Drills first, songs maybe one day. For a child, one day is forever. As an adult, you can do it the other way round: start with the songs, and let the rest make sense as you go.

Tried before and quit? So had Gary, whose verdict was simple: "This is different!"

It's called the Ridley Method, and Stephen is teaching it himself, live, for ninety minutes.

In the class you'll see:

• Why the way you were taught as a kid made it so hard
• How to start a song you love in your very first session
• The simple pattern hiding inside the songs you grew up with
• What your left hand is actually for (your teacher never said)
• How ten minutes a day beats the half hour you used to dread

It's free and it's live. You don't need a piano to join. Bring a pen, some paper and the one song you've always wanted to play.

B06.name: STATIC T-B06 black-church-choir
B06.headline: Choir singers: play the piano by ear, the way you sing
B06.message:
You already know hundreds of songs by heart. That's more of a head start at the piano than you think.

You sing them week after week. You know where every song rises, where it holds, where it lands. You can hear it straight away when the piano goes wrong.

Most people trying to learn piano don't have that. You do. What you're missing isn't an ear for music. It's knowing how those songs are built under your fingers.

Stephen Ridley plays street pianos and packed concert halls around the world. He'll tell you it was never about talent. Everything he does at a piano comes down to one thing: understanding how songs are actually built.

This might surprise a few choir singers. The person at the piano isn't doing something you can't. They're doing what you already do with your voice, with their hands instead. Singers who learn piano the right way often find it comes faster than they ever expected.

This is for you if you sing in a choir, love the music, and have always watched the person at the piano thinking: I wish that were me. Maybe you'd love to play for the choir one day. Maybe just for yourself, at home, the songs you sing every week.

Most piano courses ignore the ear you've spent years training. They sit you down with a page and drills, as if you'd never heard a song in your life. For a singer, that's backwards.

Worried it's too late? Students have started at 62 and at 70. Marie, who started at 62, calls learning "a joy".

It's called the Ridley Method, and Stephen is teaching it himself, live, for ninety minutes.

In the class you'll see:

• How the songs you sing are built, so your hands can follow your ear
• Why singers often pick up piano faster than anyone else
• What your left hand is actually for
• How to play by feel, the way you already sing
• How ten minutes a day fits around rehearsals and everything else

It's free and it's live. You don't need a piano to join. Bring a pen, some paper and the one song you've always wanted to play.

B07.name: STATIC T-B07 black-guitar-player
B07.headline: Guitar players: the piano is easier than you've been told
B07.message:
If you can strum a few songs on a guitar, you know far more about piano than you realise.

You already play by feel. You already know that a song is a few shapes going round and round, not a wall of notes. You've sat with friends and played something everyone could sing.

Then you looked at a piano and it seemed like a different, harder world. Eighty-eight keys and no idea where to put your hands.

Stephen Ridley plays street pianos and packed concert halls around the world. He'll tell you it was never about talent. Everything he does at a piano comes down to one thing: understanding how songs are actually built.

This might annoy a few piano teachers. But a guitar player usually has a better start at the piano than a beginner who's spent years reading music. You already understand songs. You just haven't seen how they sit on a keyboard.

This is for you if you play a bit of guitar, or used to, and you've always fancied the piano. If you love the sound of a piano under a song and wish you could make it yourself.

Most piano lessons throw away everything a guitar player knows. They start you on reading, drills and exercises, as if you'd never played a song in your life. That's why so many guitarists try piano once and go back to the guitar.

Tried before and gave up? So had Gary, whose verdict was simple: "This is different!"

It's called the Ridley Method, and Stephen is teaching it himself, live, for ninety minutes.

In the class you'll see:

• How the songs you strum on guitar sit on a piano
• Why guitar players often have a head start, not a handicap
• What your left hand is for (it does the job your strumming did)
• How to play piano by feel, the way you already play guitar
• How ten minutes a day is enough to make it stick

It's free and it's live. You don't need a piano to join. Bring a pen, some paper and the one song you've always wanted to play.

B08.name: STATIC T-B08 black-empty-nester
B08.headline: The kids have moved out. Now learn the piano for you
B08.message:
The kids have moved out and the house is quieter now. What if you filled it with music?

For twenty years every evening belonged to someone else. School runs, homework, lifts to practice, waiting up. You were busy in the best way, and there was never time for anything that was just yours.

Now the bedrooms are empty and the evenings are long. That quiet can feel strange. A lot of people in exactly your spot finally do the thing they put off for decades. For many of them, it's the piano.

Stephen Ridley plays street pianos and packed concert halls around the world. He'll tell you it was never about talent. Everything he does at a piano comes down to one thing: understanding how songs are actually built.

Here's something people in this chapter of life often discover. The years spent raising a family didn't make it too late. They gave you patience, focus and a head full of songs you love. That's exactly what learning piano as an adult needs.

This is for you if the kids have grown and gone and you've got time back. If you've said "when the kids are older" about the piano for years. They're older.

Most piano courses are built for children with years ahead of them: exercises now, songs much later. You've spent long enough putting things off. You want to play something you love soon, not after a year of drills.

Worried you've left it too late? Students have started at 62 and at 70. Marie, who started at 62, calls learning "a joy".

It's called the Ridley Method, and Stephen is teaching it himself, live, for ninety minutes.

In the class you'll see:

• How to start a song you love in your first session
• The simple idea underneath the songs from your whole life
• What your left hand is actually for
• How to play by feel, without reading music
• How ten minutes an evening turns a quiet house into a musical one

It's free and it's live. You don't need a piano to join. Bring a pen, some paper and the one song you've always wanted to play.

B09.name: STATIC T-B09 black-keyboard-in-closet
B09.headline: That keyboard in the closet? Learn real piano songs on it
B09.message:
You bought a keyboard. You meant to learn. Then life happened.

It's in a closet, under the bed, or leaning against a wall with a cover over it. Maybe you tried an app for a couple of weeks. Maybe you watched a few videos. Maybe you never quite started. Either way, it hasn't been switched on in months.

Every time you see it, you feel a little bit guilty.

Stephen Ridley plays street pianos and packed concert halls around the world. He'll tell you it was never about the instrument, and never about talent. Everything comes down to one thing: understanding how songs are actually built.

This might sound odd, but that keyboard is enough. You don't need a grand piano, more keys, or a better model. What was missing was never the instrument. It was a way in that starts with the songs you love.

This is for you if there's a keyboard in your home gathering dust, and you still wish you could play. If you bought it with a song in mind and never got to that song.

Apps and videos tell you which key to press next. Lights come on, you follow them, and the moment the screen goes off, you're stuck. None of them shows you how the music is built. That's why so many keyboards end up in closets.

Never played before? Neither had John. "I never played piano before in my life," John wrote. Now John plays a Roland keyboard and calls it "a blast".

It's called the Ridley Method, and Stephen is teaching it himself, live, for ninety minutes.

In the class you'll see:

• How to start the song you bought that keyboard for
• Why apps and videos leave you stuck when the screen goes off
• The simple pattern hiding inside most of the songs you love
• What your left hand is actually for
• How ten minutes a day gets that keyboard out of the closet for good

B10.name: STATIC T-B10 black-in-your-60s
B10.headline: In your 60s? Students start the piano at 62 and 70
B10.message:
"Too old to learn piano" is one of the most common things people in their sixties say. It's wrong.

You've heard it from friends. Maybe you've said it yourself. "I should have learned when I was young." "My fingers aren't what they were." "It's too late for me now."

Here's the truth: you've got things younger learners don't. Patience. Time. And a lifetime of songs you love, already in your head.

Stephen Ridley plays street pianos and packed concert halls around the world. He'll tell you it was never about talent, or age. Everything he does at a piano comes down to one thing: understanding how songs are actually built.

This might annoy anyone who thinks piano is for children. But what holds most people in their sixties back isn't their age. It's believing they have to start with years of exercises before they play anything worth hearing. That belief is the real obstacle, and it's wrong.

This is for you if you're in your sixties, you've always wanted to play, and somewhere along the way you decided you'd left it too late. If there's a song from your younger days you'd love to play for yourself.

Most piano courses are built for children with ten years ahead of them. Exercises now, music much later. You don't want "much later". You want to play something you love this year. That's a different path, and a much shorter one.

Students have started at 62 and at 70. Marie, who started at 62, calls learning "a joy". Cyd, who started at 70, calls the method "first rate".

It's called the Ridley Method, and Stephen is teaching it himself, live, for ninety minutes.

In the class you'll see:

• Why age matters far less than the order you learn in
• How to start a song you love in your very first session
• The simple idea underneath the songs from your younger days
• What your left hand is actually for
• How ten minutes a day fits easily into the week you have now

It's free and it's live. You don't need a piano to join. Bring a pen, some paper and the one song you've always wanted to play.
